options.text: By selling only by mail order
options.misconception: The ad invites shoppers to come to the store, not to order by mail.

options.text: Through newspaper ads with low prices and an invitation
By refusing to advertise at all
options.misconception: The ad itself is an advertisement, so the store did advertise.

options.text: By selling only to customers in other states
options.misconception: The ad is for a store in Allentown, selling to local shoppers.

rationales.A: The ad invites shoppers to “come and look through before your size is sold out” — it sells in the store, not by mail.
rationales.B: The ad is itself a newspaper advertisement: it lists pair after pair at reduced prices and invites shoppers to “come and look through before your size is sold out.”
rationales.C: The store printed this advertisement, so it did not refuse to advertise.
rationales.D: The ad names a store on Hamilton Street in Allentown, selling to shoppers who come in.
rationales.general:
Read the ad as evidence of how the store sold.
1. The ad lists many pairs of shoes at prices cut below what they once cost.
2. It tells shoppers to come and look before their size is sold out.
3. A store that prints prices and an invitation in the newspaper is reaching customers through advertising.
4. Nothing in the ad mentions mail order, other states, or refusing to advertise.
Remember: an advertisement is itself proof that the store advertised.

stimulus.source_note: H. Leh and Company newspaper advertisement, Allentown, Pennsylvania, 1890. Public domain.
stimulus.text: A newspaper advertisement from 1890 for H. Leh and Company, a dry goods and shoe dealer in Allentown, Pennsylvania. Under the heading “WE HAVE,” it lists pair after pair of ladies’ and gentlemen’s shoes at reduced prices — $4.50 shoes now $2.95, $3 shoes now $2 — and invites shoppers to “come and look through before your size is sold out.”
